newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing trial penalty goes to summations.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing trial penalty goes to summations.

text.p: Lawyers for convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh put a human face on him, but face a challenge in Thursday's closing arguments in the penalty phase in trying to save him from the death sentence, legal experts said.

"This is going to be an unusual case in which the actual rhetorical power of the closing arguments is going to mean a lot," said Robert Precht, Director of Public Service at the University of Michigan Law School.
The defence rested its case on Wednesday in the sentencing phase of the bombing trial.

The jury last week found McVeigh guilty of the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in which 168 people died. Its members will begin their task of deciding if he should be executed or spend the rest of his life in prison.
The prosecution has asked for a death sentence, while the defence since Friday has been trying to persuade the jury of seven men and five women to spare his life.
"The death penalty is the prosecution's to lose and they aren't going to lose it," said Scott Robinson, a Denver trial attorney who has been analysing the trial.
While many of the relatives of people who perished in the bombing believe only a death sentence will satisfy justice, the opinion is not unanimous.
"It's not going to bring my daughter back. It's not going to bring me any peace of mind," said Marsha Kight, whose 23-year-old daughter, Frankie Merrell, died in the bombing.
On Wednesday McVeigh's parents pleaded for their son's life.
"He is not the monster he has been portrayed as," said his mother, Mildred Frazer, reading tearfully from a statement. "He was a child any mother could be proud of."
His father, William McVeigh, narrated 10 minutes of family home movies, showing a young "Timmy" diving into a pool and playing in the back yard.

"I think the defence succeeded in humanising McVeigh and conveying to the jury the sense this is a man who led a life that has positive value, that he made a contribution to society in other aspects of his life apart from the bombing episode," said Christopher Mueller, a law professor at the University of Colorado.
But the problem, Robinson said, is that McVeigh's lack of a criminal record and decency as a young man may very well be outweighed by the enormity of suffering caused by the bombing.

"This case is so fraught with irony. Unlike most first degree murder cases where the defendant is someone utterly without redeeming social values ... Here we have someone who was a helpful student, not a bully, had a sense of humour. They have enormous mitigation, but the aggravation is so overwhelming that it doesn't matter," Robinson said.

EX-army buddies testified that McVeigh was a model soldier; teachers said he was a good student and the defence also focused on the government's raid on the Branch Davidian cult in Waco, Tex. on April 19, 1993.

The defence has not admitted that McVeigh was responsible for the bombing. But McVeigh's lawyers have portrayed the Gulf War veteran as a man deeply troubled by the deaths at Waco, who blamed federal officials for a fire at the compound that killed cult leader David Koresh and about 80 of his followers.

"I think the defence diluted the impact of the evidence that tended to humanise him by putting on this evidence about Waco," said Precht who was also a defence attorney in the World Trade Centre bombing trials.

"It veered dangerously into suggesting that he had a political motivation to do what he did and that seems to be inconsistent with a strategy of humanising, making him appear to be someone who for all his misdeeds is still a human being that deserves mercy," Precht said.
